PROCEDURE IN DEALING WITH DIVORCE BILLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I rise on a question of privilege. I have had a communication from my constituents who are very much concerned about the present world situation, and particularly the situation here in Canada. They feel that our time here is not being properly occupied, when for two, three or four nights we use the services of this highest court in the land to discuss matters which concern perhaps two or three or four hundred individuals, regarding their marital relationship, when we could be discussing matters of great concern to the 14 million people in Canada. They have asked me, and I ask through you, sir, whether the government would not give some consideration to calling in the law officers of the crown and others who may be required in order that we may cut some of the red tape which is holding up the proceedings of this chamber at this time of stress and strain in the minds and hearts of all our people.
It does not matter if we have to stay here until Christmas; let us divorce ourselves for another year or two from the bills to which I refer and get down to the hard facts of cold-blooded business so far as Canada is concerned.
My specific point of privilege, Mr. Speaker, is to ask those charged with responsibility, and all the help that they have around them here, there and beyond, and some over on this side, to get together and slash some of this red tape so that we may get on with the business of Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION OF THE MACKENZIE KING TRUST ACCOUNT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a few remarks that I think should be made at this stage of the bill. I am sure that no one will be disposed to object to any generosity shown by the late Mr. King to the people of Canada. Indeed I think everyone will be inclined not only to agree that the financial objects of his will are praiseworthy, but also to confirm the general sentiments and objectives that he himself expressed, that although he had done much for this nation, it too had done much for him and had been generous to him, and that it was fitting that he should make some gift to the nation which had elevated him for so long to the office of first citizen and done so much for him while he occupied that office. I am sure we shall all agree that that was a worthy and proper motive.
But such enthusiasm as we may have for this proposal should not blind us to the realization that it is not likely to be carried out without some considerable expense to the taxpayer. After all, we have but recently had under consideration a project for a house for the present and future prime ministers which was approved by parliament on the

basis of one estimate, but which was realized only at a cost to the taxpayers of well over $500,000 more than the amount first indicated. I think we should beware lest this project in connection with the home of a past prime minister should also cost the taxpayers vastly more than is at first indicated.
The right hon. gentleman who is the leader of the present government, in the answer he gave to my question yesterday, said that the sum provided under the will of the late Mr. King will not be sufficient to carry out the full cost of his monument, and that the public treasury is to be diminished also to bear the cost of bringing to their full fruition Mr. King's bequest and his ideas as to how his house should be used. Therefore we should make some inquiries as to how the project is to be administered and how much the annual cost to the taxpayer will be.
I should like the Prime Minister to indicate, if he will, just how this cost is to be met. Will it be met by way of an annual item in the estimates under the federal district commission, or under the dominion archives?
I think we should receive further particulars when in committee. We shall have an opportunity to ask questions at that time. I should like to know what the estimated cost of the alterations is. What staff will be necessary to operate the research centre? What will be the cost of acquiring and installing and storing the various historical materials? These are subjects to which our minds should be directed, so that we may know how much the actual bequest of cash made by the late Mr. King will fall short of the requirements necessary to carry out the project envisaged in this bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION OF THE MACKENZIE KING TRUST ACCOUNT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add just a word to what the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) has said. As the hon. member has stated, there are two aspects of this matter. The first is the gift to the people of Canada, which we respect and welcome, and the other is the expenditure of money by the people of Canada, in connection with which I think we should be fully informed.

That house was left to him by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. King himself bequeathed it to the government just as he had previously given his summer cottage at Kingsmere. He also willed a few hundred thousand dollars to be spent on the upkeep of these properties, something the leaders of the Conservative party at that 80709-197
Laurier House
time unfortunately never did. It is unfortunate that former leaders of the Conservative party did not show the same generosity on their departure. The Right Hon. Mr. Bennett went to Europe and left his money to England instead of to Canada. That is the difference * between the two parties. They were led by two bachelors; one of them was attached to his country while the other was not.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION OF THE MACKENZIE KING TRUST ACCOUNT
speechtext:
Is the Minister of Public Works in a position to make any estimate as to what it will cost to put this house in proper repair? As I suggested yesterday, I do not think that any very expensive work is required on the outside of the building. If my reading of the portion of the will which was placed on the record by the Prime Minister is correct, I think it was the late prime minister's desire that the interior of the house should remain pretty much as it is now. That is to say, it would not need a great deal of expenditure on structural alterations as was the case with the new residence of the Prime Minister.
Perhaps the Minister of Public Works could give us some information that would be useful in the light of the suggestion made a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Kamloops. Can the minister indicate approximately what it is proposed to do, and what the cost will be? I do not think a very large outlay is needed at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION OF THE MACKENZIE KING TRUST ACCOUNT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I must admit that after looking through the bill I would assume that our duties with respect to Laurier house will be to maintain it in a good state of repair. We have not visited the place to make an estimate as to what is actually needed, but as it is an old building I am sure we shall have to spend money every year to maintain it in a good state of repair.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION OF THE MACKENZIE KING TRUST ACCOUNT
speechtext:
I am interested in this question, as I know many other hon. members are. As the hon. member for Greenwood has said, the matter is approachable from two angles. First there is the gift to the nation. So far as that is concerned, it is welcome. But there is also the question of the upkeep or expense to the nation which may be involved in carrying out the terms of this bequest. We have had experience recently in embarking on projects in connection with houses without knowing what the total cost was going to be, and then having the unpleasant shock, which has given rise to unpleasantness all

Laurier House
round, of finding that the cost 'has greatly exceeded what we were led to believe at first would be the approximate figure. I can hardly credit the fact that the government would actually be introducing legislation to go ahead and set up this project without some estimate of the cost which will be involved. I think the Minister of Public Works said that they had not looked into it at all, that they do not know what the cost will be. I am certain that the minister would not wish to make that approach to legislation. I hope I misunderstood him. I hope I misinterpreted him, and I trust there is some plan of the way in which the project is to be administered. I should like to ask the Minister of Public Works whether any plan has yet been made and any estimate prepared of any structural alterations, either interior or exterior, to place the house in such a condition that it can fulfil the terms of the bequest.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION OF THE MACKENZIE KING TRUST ACCOUNT
speechtext: If I understand correctly our position under this measure, it is to maintain the house in a good state of repair. We will consider Laurier house in the same way as we consider other public buildings in Ottawa belonging to the federal government. Estimates will come before the house. If the repairs are minor in character, the cost will be taken out of the general vote. They will be examined by the treasury board, and reported in the Auditor General's report. If they are extensive repairs to the building, there will be a special estimate. I intend to wait to see in what condition the house is. Before going into this property we had to accept ownership of it. This having been done not long ago, I did not think it was my duty to interfere with the property and have estimates prepared in advance of the bill, so I am not in a position to give the amount to be expended nor to go into the details.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION OF THE MACKENZIE KING TRUST ACCOUNT
speechtext: Perhaps we have a fundamentally different approach to this problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION OF THE MACKENZIE KING TRUST ACCOUNT
speechtext: That of course does happen.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION OF THE MACKENZIE KING TRUST ACCOUNT
speechtext: Based on past experience, however, I think we should be more careful. Are we to take it from the reply the minister has made that no preliminary inspection has been made of the house, and that no preliminary plans have been drawn up or any preliminary decision made as to whether it will even be necessary to effect any structural alteration either to the interior or to the exterior of the building to place it in such a condition that it can fulfil the purpose of the bequest? Have any such preliminary inspections or plans been made?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION OF THE MACKENZIE KING TRUST ACCOUNT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, probably the house will have to be redecorated, and we shall have to do some work on the exterior. We are not going to change Laurier house into another kind of structure, or enlarge it. We are going to try to keep it the way it is, in order that it may be the memorial it is intended to be. As to the expense, I will invite my good friend to my office some morning and we will look into all the details. We will go over the rooms and get some expert to give the hon. member the exact amount needed to do the necessary work.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION OF THE MACKENZIE KING TRUST ACCOUNT
speechtext: I can assure the minister I shall be pleased to accept his invitation whenever it is extended, but I think it might have been more timely if the invitation had been extended before the bill was introduced rather than after, so that we could have had that information before us. I should like to ask the minister a further question. What staff will be necessary to operate the research centre under the dominion archivist when the scheme is operating?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION OF THE MACKENZIE KING TRUST ACCOUNT
speechtext:
There has has been no preliminary plan made as to that. The will was communicated to the government. The government felt it was proper to accept the bequest, and that it was proper to come before parliament and recommend that the dominion archivist be put in charge of Laurier house, and that he be assisted by a curator to conserve the property. I know that up to the present time there has been some preliminary inspection, and I am told that something is being done about some bit of electric wiring in the house which, for the safety of the premises, should be attended to. I was told that was all that was required as a matter of urgency. There has been no plan determined. As a matter of fact the inventory of the contents of the house to be turned over by the executors to the government has not yet been completed. It is still in process.
The title to the real estate was conveyed to the government as of the first of January, but there is a representative of the executors still on the premises, and, together with Mr. Handy, who is a civil servant and was Mr. King's private secretary, he is drawing up the inventory of contents which will remain a part of the property. The executors and Mr. Handy did look over the house to see if there was anything urgently required for its preservation. I was informed that all that was urgently required-and it was being attended to-was some bit of wiring in the electric lighting system that might have constituted a danger.

With respect to the manner in which the house will be used, that will depend upon what is subsequently determined. I think the dominion archivist is a gentleman who enjoys the confidence of all Canadian students, and I think that Canadian students and the Canadian public will be satisfied that he will not recommend anything in the way of facilities to be provided to students that would not be worth what it is going to cost the country. This bill is the preliminary step. The suggestion that is being made is that Laurier house be heated and maintained by the Department of Public Works, that the dominion archivist be in control, and that he have a curator under him to look after the place.
A question has been asked as to when the house is to be open to the public. I was told recently on behalf of the executors that they did not think it could be opened to the public until quite late this summer, that they are still proceeding with their sorting out of the contents of the house, and that it is not possible to be specific about that matter.
With respect to the grounds, the recommendation is that they be maintained as a part of the parkway system that the federal district commission maintains in Ottawa. Whenever anything is required that will be beyond the cost of the ordinary upkeep, there will have to be an appropriation by parliament. There will have to be a recommendation to parliament, at which time the plans and details will be communicated to parliament. Unless parliament is going to say this bequest should not be accepted, it is necessary to proceed in this gradual fashion and not attempt to communicate to parliament any suggestions at this time as to what would be the best way to take advantage of this property as a research facility for students, but to obtain the considered recommendation of the dominion archivist. That is what the government plans to do.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, May 15, consideration in committee of Bill No. 79, respecting Indians-Mr. Harris (Grey-Bruce) -Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
On section 110-Sale of lands of enfranchised Indians.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AND CONSOLIDATION
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: Can the minister assure us that he will not see these reserves become pinpointed with white settlers? Just before adjournment last evening I made a few remarks on this section and pointed out that danger. Will the minister comment on that point?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: AMENDMENT AND CONSOLIDATION
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
We recognize that some Indians might be concerned1 about this section. Until they have read its provisions they might conclude that there could be pinpointing of reserves, as my hon. friend has termed it; 'but when this section is read along with a previous section it becomes perfectly obvious that there are several safeguards to prevent that from happening. In the first instance, land must be allotted to an Indian. That action is taken by the band council, with the approval of the minister. At a subsequent time, if he chooses to become enfranchised, he may apply to the band council and to the minister for the privilege of retaining the ownership of the land which has been allotted to him. Then there is a further safeguard that, nevertheless, he does not obtain title to that land until ten years after that date. It is true that at that point he may then sell it to anyone he chooses. This is a change from the old act, designed to meet the objections of some Indians, and in particular an objection made before the special committee by a distinguished former member of the Six Nations from Brantford, that it was unfair to the Indian that he should have land allotted to him, work on it and improve it, and that when he wants to become enfranchised-it is admittedly our policy to encourage him to do that-he should nevertheless be penalized at that point and be restrained from becoming enfranchised because he would then have to sell his land to a limited number of people, namely, the members of that particular band.
Strong representations were made before the special committee by Brigadier Martin that that was unfair. Similar representations have been made to me since that time by individual Indians. Other compassionate representations were made, one of which was that Indians, as my hon. friend1 has said, on the outskirts of a reserve might wish to

become enfranchised and one could not distinguish whether they were on or off the reserve. But it was decided to continue the provisions of the present act, which are there but which have not been used, in such a way that an Indian could become enfranchised and at the same time reside on his land on the reserve. As I say, we have built up all these safeguards; the initial allotment which must be approved by the minister and the band council, the application for enfranchisement which must be approved by the minister, the application for land which must be approved by the band council and the minister, and then the ten year waiting period. So I think under those circumstances the numbers who will take advantage of this will be small. If there are some, they should have this right.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AND CONSOLIDATION
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: I do not think that people living off the reserve should stipulate to Indians who are living on the reserve, as in the case mentioned by the minister. I do know of an Indian who has a very good farm, but he cannot will his land to his daughters if they marry non-Indians. I know that situation has arisen several times, and it does appear to be a little bit hard on those persons. I know of one Indian who is ini that situation, and he cannot will his land to his daughters because they have all married whites. He lives north of the Grand river, as a matter of fact, bordering on white land, I suppose in certain cases it cannot be helped, but as I mentioned before, I hope it will not result in pinpointing the reserve. I do not believe the minister has ever had anyone come to him from the Six Nations council making this request.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in connection with the preamble and the general substance of the bill as amended I suggest to the minister that in order to protect the rights of Indians covered by this act, no Indian should be denied recourse to the courts under the provisions of this bill. I ask the minister whether or not he would be prepared, having already taken the stand that there is no denial of recourse to the courts, to accept an amendment which reads as follows:
Nothing in this act or elsewhere shall in any way be deemed to remove, abridge or otherwise restrict the rights of Indians to full access to the courts of the land, and every Indian and every band of Indians shall have the full right to appeal to the appropriate court of the province which would otherwise have jurisdiction, from any decision of the minister hereunder.
Indian Act
I believe such a provision would be salutary in its effects. It would assure to the Indians a position of responsibility, coupled with an opportunity to preserve their rights against anything which they believed to be administrative lawlessness.
If there is one thing more than any other that I think should be assured to the Indians, it is the right to do what all the rest of us can do-to seek out the king's courts with a view to protection against what they consider to be wrongs. There would certainly be no harm to the administration of the act. The court would have no authority to review discretionary orders. The power of review would be the power to remedy wrongdoing wherever wrongdoing existed.
I make this request of the minister in the interests of the more than 100,000 Indians of this country. They should not be placed in the position of having their rights determined not in courts of law but by administrative officials or by the minister. Nothing is more important today than preserving the full rights of the individual under the law.
If my view be correct, we have in this country 125,000 native born Canadians who cannot, if injustice be done to them, seek out the king's courts for the preservation of their rights. If the minister's view be correct that the Indian has that right-I say with great deference that the Indian has no such right today under this act-then the amendment that I ask him to accept will add nothing to the rights of these people. If on the other hand my view be correct, then it will actually assure the Indian of something that over the years he has been asking for, namely, the rights that Canadian citizens and others who are not Canadians or British subjects enjoy-recourse to the king's courts.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: AMENDMENT AND CONSOLIDATION
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
this brings up a subject which has been a matter of considerable astonishment to the minister since he took over the administration of the Indian Act. I never knew that an Indian could not sue in the courts of Canada in the same way as any other person-

subtopic: AMENDMENT AND CONSOLIDATION
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Against administrative
order?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: AMENDMENT AND CONSOLIDATION
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
I did not know that when I became minister of this department; I do not know it now. Indians have the right to sue in courts, and have been exercising those rights at all times that I am aware of, and nothing in the present Indian Act, or in the revised Indian Act now before the house, would abridge that right in any way. For that reason I would reject the amendment, not only because it might

Indian Act
be considered unnecessary, tout because it leaves the inference that in the present act, or in the revised act, there may be, or there may have been, an abridgement of that right.
This matter was referred to by the hon. member for Lake Centre in his speech on Bill No. 267 last summer, when he said that an Indian, or a band in Saskatchewan-I am not sure which it is now-had been refused the right to sue the crown. As he said yesterday, there was a case in Saskatchewan in which damages were assessed against the crown by a court, I think it was in 1935. He said yesterday that as a result of that judgment others had been refused a fiat since to sue the crown. Now, both after he made the speech last year and yesterday I asked for and had a search made of our records, and with the exception of one case that I have been able to find, not in Saskatchewan, but in Manitoba, we have no record whatever of a fiat having been refused. It may well be-my hon. friend said he was counsel, and of course he knows-it may well be that there have been other cases, but if he was referring to the Manitoba case, then I am quite prepared to understand the point he made. The one case in Manitoba is well known to members from that province.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AND CONSOLIDATION
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
The Sinclair case; I
know the Manitoba one.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: AMENDMENT AND CONSOLIDATION
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
In that case
there had been certain transactions over forty years ago, which gave rise to debates in this house spread over a number of years. In the end a statute was passed by parliament settling the matter, at least in the view of those who were then responsible for the government of Canada, after negotiation and some form of settlement. Ultimately when it was sought to sue the crown on the basis of the prior matters having to do with that band, a fiat was refused in 1936 because parliament had already dealt with the matter and had presumably disposed of it.
So far as I know, that is the only case in which an Indian or a band council has been refused a fiat in recent times. There may have been some many years ago. When I visited Saskatchewan I met representative Indians, both in the northern part and in the southern part, and I did find an opinion there that they were not free to sue the crown. I told them that I thought they were more progressive than that. They were Canadian citizens; they had all the rights so far as access to the courts was concerned that I could think of, and that if anyone in the hall wanted to sue the minister or the crown all he had to do was to go outside and retain a solicitor to do it. We have not had any lawsuits since. I have repeated that statement in every meeting that I have had 
with the Indians. The right to sue the crown is well known by the Indians. Let there be no mistake about that.
I agree that there have been many complaints about maladministration, and there have been occasions in the past when perhaps if they had taken action they might have obtained damages in cases other than the one I have referred to. But these matters are adjusted. If complaints are made in or out of parliament, the Indian affairs branch does try to meet those complaints and in some way to make compensation for what might appear to be injustices. Nevertheless, I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that lawsuits are going on at this moment between Indians and the crown. There is no bar to them except the obtaining of a fiat, and that, as my hon. friend has pointed out, may be removed by action of this parliament; I think it is on the order paper. For that reason, sir, I would not want to give any credence to the suggestion that in the past there has been any objection to an Indian taking action against the crown, nor would I want to import into this bill the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Lake Centre.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AND CONSOLIDATION
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
I thank the minister for his explanation. I know of the case in Manitoba. The solicitor in the case was the late Bichard Mulcaster, K.C. The case in Saskatchewan to which I referred was in 1936, and was an application made by him, with myself to be counsel, in the case of the Mistawasis Indians. The application was made to the Department of Justice.
The minister referred to the case in Manitoba. I know the facts in connection with it. Indeed I read the debates in parliament long before I came to this house. If I recollect aright, the late Mr. Bradbury, M.P., of Selkirk, Manitoba, made a lengthy speech about millions of dollars that allegedly were owing to the band there by reason of the appropriation of certain lands in Manitoba that were taken over by the crown many years before. Again, speaking from recollection, I seem to recall that an action was started in the Exchequer Court of Canada about 1908 or 1909-the minister may correct me if I am wrong-and the action never came to trial. Is that not so?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: AMENDMENT AND CONSOLIDATION
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AND CONSOLIDATION
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO BAND FUNDS
speechtext:
Yes. I am speaking from recollection. I know that case very well. But the minister has not grasped the significance of what I have in mind. I do not say that an Indian has not the right in ordinary matters of recourse to the courts, but what I say is he has not the right today, except in the specified sections that allow aft appeal to the Exchequer Court of Canada, to appeal

against administrative orders, except those specially covered by this act. In other words, he is in the position of being subject to order and direction under the act, except in so far as the three or four sections which allow an appeal to the exchequer court are concerned. He is in the position of a person whose rights may be determined, whose responsibilities may be declared, but at the same time, whether acceptable to him or not, he has no recourse to the courts, either by action, by prerogative right of mandamus or prohibition or certiorari.
These are the cases that I have in mind. These are the matters on which I am asking that the Indians be placed in a position equal to the rest of us. These are the rights. The right of appeal against an order of the king's ministry should be preserved to the individual. There is a case in that regard, reported I think in 1940 Supreme Court Reports, where in Saskatchewan a minister of the crown failed to discharge his responsibility under the natural resources act. The individual whose rights were interfered with had no right of action against the crown. I point out that he was not an Indian. His counsel carried the matter to the courts, by the use of the king's prerogative right to preserve the king's subjects from the tyranny of the king's ministers. That matter came before the court of appeal in Saskatchewan, and the court decided that every person within the king's dominions has the right of appeal to the king, and that the king in turn will ask that his ministers or his servants shall not diminish, interfere with or abrogate the rights of the subjects.
That is what I have m mind under this act, where tremendous powers are vested in the minister. Those powers can be exercised by the minister without right of appeal to the courts, except under certain specific sections which grant that right of appeal. For instance section 47 refers to authority conferred upon the minister by other sections, one of which deals with the testamentary disposition of property, the descent of property and the like.
Section 47 says that a decision of the minister made in the exercise of the jurisdiction or authority conferred upon him by section 42, 43 or 46 may, within two months from the date thereof, be appealed by any person affected thereby to the Exchequer Court of Canada, if the amount in controversy in the appeal exceeds $500, or if the minister consents to an appeal. Then, the second subsection states that the judges of the exchequer court may make rules, and so on.
Indian Act
There are a few provisions in which appeals are allowed, but many sections deny the right of appeal from the minister. There can be no appeal from the minister's decision unless, as in section 47, the power is actually granted. I am asking the minister to grant to Indians affected by administrative regulations or rulings the right of appeal to the king's courts, in order to preserve the rights of the individual against the possibility of injustices on the part of the minister or his advisers.
The minister takes the broad and general view that there is a right of appeal to the courts by Indians. Certainly, they have a general right; but within the Indian Act they are restricted and are denied an appeal, except where it is specifically given. There is no disagreement between us that an Indian can appeal if a decision in a criminal case is made against him, or if he wishes to take action in the courts. But the right of appeal under the Indian Act, in so far as administrative matters are concerned or, indeed, in so far as declaratory orders by the minister are concerned, is denied, and that right exists only where specifically given, as set out in section 47.
I am glad the minister has brought the matter up in this way. There is never any disagreement between us that the Indian has a general right of recourse to the courts. The disagreement arises when it is realized that, under the Indian Act, except where granted the special right of appeal, he has no rights in the courts of the country. If he had the right, as the minister insists, there would have been no section 47 granting him a specific right in certain circumstances. Owing to the fact that in respect of various types of orders under the act that right of recourse is not available, I made application to the minister to give consideration along the lines suggested.

Last fall after the passage of the act the first set of regulations were brought into effect. Of the 49,404 cars sold there were 12,745 sold on instalment buying in that month. There has been a steady increase

Consumer Credit
in the sales of cars since the regulations were introduced, but there has been quite a noticeable decrease in the percentage of cars sold under instalment buying. The other figures are a little more difficult to ascertain because the dominion bureau of statistics takes quite a bit longer to assemble them from all the trades concerned. Members undoubtedly have studied the figures given in the report covering the last quarter of 1950. Since the last quarter of 1950 included a month in which there were no consumer credit regulations as well as two months in which there were consumer credit regulations, the picture perhaps is not shown very accurately. The new report on consumer credit will be out in the next two or three days. From the manuscript, which unfortunately is not completed, I can pick out certain representative sales. These sales are given in percentages.
For example, in the period October to December inclusive of last year 68-7 per cent of all department store sales were for cash, 13 per cent on instalment buying, and 18-3 per cent on monthly charge accounts. We now have the figures for department stores for this quarter. They show an increase to 69 per cent in cash sales, quite a marked drop of 2-3 per cent to 10-7 per cent in instalment buying, and an increase in charge accounts to 20-3 per cent. Therefore there has been a drop in instalment buying through department stores, which are one of the principal methods of sale by instalment and credit accounts, a slight rise in cash sales and a rise in charge accounts.
The amendments in the present bill are quite minor. The first amendment has to do with a fairly new device used mainly by department stores. Most department stores have charge accounts which people are expected to settle at the end of each month. If they are in arrears two months of course the store takes the usual credit action. I have a table here showing the extent of days outstanding in department stores. For December, 1948, the figure for average days outstanding on charge accounts is 65, for 1949 it is 67, and for 1950 it is 71. However, these charge accounts are not instalment buying in the ordinary sense.
As well as ordinary instalment buying where a definite contract is arranged for each piece of equipment or furniture sold, department stores and other large stores have set up revolving credit accounts, six month accounts, where the customer establishes with the company a line of credit. Take, for example, an individual who is able to establish to the satisfaction of the credit manager that he can pay a line of credit of $240 in a

six month period. He is expected to make an immediate down payment of one-sixth, $40. If he does not buy anything from the store that month there is no need for him to make the next payment. If he makes any purchase whatsoever, then he must at the end of the first month pay the second one-sixth, or $40. That system is carried on throughout the six month period.
The loophole, so far as consumer credit was concerned, however, was that there was no conditional sale of the particular article which he might have purchased. He pays his $40 down, and then a week or two weeks later may decide to buy a small stove, for example. The stove is sold to him purely on the credit card which he has for his revolving credit account. The lawyers felt that was a loophole, and that the definition of conditional sale should be expanded to cover revolving credit accounts. The problem is a minor one because these revolving credit accounts limit the credit to six months whereas under our present regulations we allow conditional sales to be made over a twelve month period. It is true that the down payment in this respect would be only one-sixth, that is, the first month's payment, rather than the one-third which we ask for under a conditional sale, but that one-third of course applies to the whole year. Therefore the actual loophole to be closed is a very small one.
The second loophole which has been disclosed is the matter of payment under a contract for hire of consumer goods. There has always been a perfectly legitimate business in renting refrigerators and household furnishings of various sorts for short periods to people who may be transients or only want to rent furniture for a while. However, since the introduction of consumer credit regulations, both in Canada and the United States, a new device has appeared. Let us take a television set costing $600. Under our present regulations the purchaser would have to pay $200 down and pay the balance of $400 in the next year. There have been some merchants who have said to customers:	We will rent you this $600
television set for the next thirty months. You will not have any down payment to make. You will just pay $20 a month for the next thirty months, and at the end of that time we will cut the rental rate down to $1 a year.
This practice is not very widespread yet in this country. However, it became quite widespread in the United States. They stopped it by not authorizing such rental agreement beyond the fifteen months which they allow for conditional sales. They also required a one-third deposit by the person

renting on which the company must pay the customer interest. Therefore they have solved the problem quite nicely in that way. That does not in any way affect the perfectly bona fide rental of ordinary household furniture for three or four months such as conducted in most of the large cities by furniture stores.
The next amendment has to do with contracts for work and labour. Let me give two examples. First there is the example of a man taking a car to a garage and having a new engine installed. The claim was made that that was a work contract and that the regulations requiring one-third down and payment within a year did not apply. The same sort of argument was raised where a plumber would instal an automatic washing machine. He would supply the washing machine and instal it, and then claim that since his labour was involved it was a labour contract which did not come within the scope of this legislation. That, of course, was most unfair to ordinary appliance dealers and stores selling the same article, and being forced to sell it under this consumer credit act. So that, too, has been brought into the amendment with the thought that if it is desired the labour can be separated from the material content of the consumer goods involved, and the payments for labour can be whatever the person supplying the labour wishes, but the actual sale of the consumer goods content will be subject to these regulations.
The third change has been the requirement that loan companies who are not directly concerned with sales but who advance money to finance sales must keep records of loans for the purchase of consumer goods in the same manner as we require of the stores who actually sell the goods. The last amendment is to authorize the officers not only to inspect books but to take books to court if necessary, providing they must be returned within 90 days.

I am in full sympathy with this bill, and I support it wholeheartedly. It has been drawn to my attention that a little injustice is being done to the motor car dealers of British Columbia. They cite their experience since this measure was introduced. In order to give some indication of what they have in mind, I shall quote briefly from one letter which is typical of the others. It reads:
The recent credit regulations have certainly accomplished the aim of the government to restrict unwarranted spending. They have also put a serious obstacle in the way for a man that is compelled to purchase transportation in order to enable him to get to and from his work. They do not hinder a man of means, who can purchase a new car each year, but they do seriously hurt the worker that must have essential transportation.
The letter continues along that line. It points out that the generally high freight rate to British Columbia severely handicaps British Columbia dealers, and puts them at a disadvantage on each car that is sold. For example, the freight from Windsor to Vernon, B.C., is approximately $300, whereas the freight on the same car delivered to Ottawa or Toronto would be $30 or $50. I believe the dealers have approached the government about this matter. They believe that there should be three distinct districts created for the purpose of the credit regulations on automobiles, and they ask for relief on that basis. They would divide Canada into three zones, one west of the great lakes, Ontario and Quebec, and the maritimes. They have asked that the zone west of the great lakes and the maritimes be given relief to the

extent of a forty per cent down payment with fifteen months to pay. It is felt that credit regulations covering the whole of Canada, as they do, are unfair because they work a hardship on the purchaser of a car in British Columbia who would have to pay at least $125 or $150 more by way of down payment than the purchaser of the same car in Ottawa or Toronto.
With that in mind, they suggest that the government should give serious consideration to setting up these three zones now. I do not know if that can be done at this stage of the .bill, or whether the parliamentary assistant has investigated the matter and found no practical solution. I do feel, however, that an extension of time should be given to those who are in the west or in the maritimes, and who have to purchase a car. In my riding the main source of income is the fruit, on which payments are made twice a year. Naturally, those people with a monthly income can meet their monthly payments much more easily than people who receive their income in one or two payments during the year. For that reason, I would ask the department and the parliamentary assistant to give serious consideration to the granting of the request of the association of motor dealers of British Columbia.

Mr. Chairman, I am particularly pleased to hear the member for Yale speak so well of the consumer credit regulations generally, because he has extensive knowledge of their workings in his own retail businesses. The problem of the impact of these regulations on British Columbia has been raised with the minister by the automobile association. Two points arise immediately. Of course, the argument raised applies only to Canadian cars. I am told that British-made cars are laid down in Vancouver at prices lower than any other place in Canada, including Halifax, because they generally come out as deck loads on the timber ships returning to B.C. The first step, therefore, in any regulation to cover this situation would have to be the singling out of whether the car was of Canadian or British make.
The other point it raises is the fact that once you try to get zones for consumer credit regulations based on independent things such as freight rates or local sales tax-the sales tax of three per cent in British Columbia is another factor which raises the price-it makes the regulations very difficult to administer. This time our regulations are even simpler than those in effect during the last war when we had a variety of rates for different commodities. The retail trade found it very difficult to keep abreast of these
Consumer Credit
various rates, the various types of down payment and terms of repayment. It was for this reason that, after consultation with the retail trade of Canada, the department decided to make the regulations as simple as possible. In the case of a car it is a half down, and twelve months to pay; in the case of other consumer goods, one-third down and twelve months to pay. For these reasons the department decided that it would be best to have one national set of rules. Once you extended such considerations to the purchase of Canadian-made cars, you would I suppose have to give similar concessions to the sale of British cars in Winnipeg or Regina. Then, of course, you would be led into concessions to other heavy goods in which the freight rate is a substantial item, such as stoves and refrigerators.
The other point raised by the hon. member is already covered in the regulations. It is provided that in the case of a farmer, fisherman or other person whose annual income is derived mainly in one or two lump sums, he can make payment in that fashion, provided the terms of payment are still within the year mentioned in the regulations.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. J. Mcllrailh (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the new
Department of Defence Production was set up at the start of the current fiscal year it took over the task of the procurement of supplies for the three armed services, which function up to that time had been performed by the Canadian Commercial Corporation. The corporation was then left with the task of carrying out transactions for other governments and of attending to certain bulk purchases. The change in its duties was quite considerable and as a result certain changes are required in the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act.
These changes do not involve matters of principle, they involve only matters of clarification. Perhaps it would be more desirable if I dealt with them in committee, but at this stage I could indicate what they are. The first amendment simply clarifies the definition of minister. There was some doubt as to whether the next amendment was legally necessary, but it does make clear that the corporation has the legal capacity to perform the functions authorized by other acts of parliament. The third amendment clarifies the language used with respect to the revolving fund authorized under the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act. It does not add any new power to what was stated to be included when the section was originally passed by this house, but it does clarify the language.
The next provision is to permit a smaller quorum at the meetings of the directors, reducing the quorum to three. The number of directors is being reduced from nine to six. The act authorizes a board of directors made up of from five to nine with a quorum of five, which will be reduced to three by this amendment. The concluding section makes it possible for certain employees of the corporation to be brought under the benefits of the Civil Service Superannuation Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
I want to
ask a general question about the relation between the Canadian Commercial Corporation and the Department of National Defence having regard to what actually happens when the Canadian Commercial Corporation, on behalf of the Department of National Defence, lets a contract for the preparation, construction and manufacture of goods for the Department of National Defence. What I want to be clear about is, what is the division of function? The Department of National Defence reaches the conclusion that it wants certain things, and it asks the Canadian Commercial Corporation to procure them. This matter has arisen in the public accounts committee. From that point on I am anxious to know exactly where the responsibility lies. I find it a little difficult to understand. Indeed it seemed to me there was perhaps a danger of duplication. I should like to be informed just what the division of responsibility is from that point on.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there has been a change in the system of defence buying, particularly in. those purchases that require new facilities or new arrangements to produce. The Department of Defence Production has been established, and a good many of the duties formerly performed by the Canadian Commercial Corporation have been taken over by the production branches of the Department of Defence Production. For instance, the aircraft branch of the department is responsible for all procurement in connection with the aircraft program. Defence construction is handled apart from the Canadian Commercial Corporation. A separate crown company is responsible for defence construction. Similarly the gun division handles all procurement in connection with guns except for foreign orders. Orders from foreign governments are routed through the Canadian Commercial Corporation for the reason that production has to be financed for a time before outside payments are received.
The scope of the corporation has been reduced. A number of men formerly

employed by the corporation have been taken over by the procurement branches. For instance, Mr. Trethewey, formerly head of the aircraft branch for Canadian Commercial Corporation, is now one of the heads of the aircraft production branch.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: I should like to ask a question at that point. On the face of it, it appears that administrative expenditure for 1950-51 for the Canadian Commercial Corporation, if I understand the matter correctly, is about $400,000 larger. Is the change that the minister is describing just taking place now so that it will alter that? The figures given by the parliamentary assistant show that.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: The change in organization took place in the late months of 1950. The Department of Defence Production was only officially organized as of April 1, but its activities began to function during the late months of 1950. If my hon. friend will note the size of the contracts placed by the Canadian Commercial Corporation he will understand why in that year there was a considerable increase in staff and in expenditures. I presume for the year 1951-52 the volume handled by the Canadian Commercial Corporation and the expenses involved will be down instead of up.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: What comes from the minister's answer is that there are now really three organizations. There is the Department of National Defence, the Canadian Commercial Corporation, and the Department of Defence Production, and as I understand it the duty of defence production is to do a good deal of the work formerly done by the Canadian Commercial Corporation. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, that is correct.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
My basic question still remains. Just what is the division of responsibility between the Department of National Defence, which gives the order so to speak, and the Canadian Commercial Corporation or defence production which I suppose we can say does the arranging to get the goods? As I understand the matter in the public accounts committee, the Department of National Defence naturally is deeply interested in what is being obtained, and I presume in a way it is the Anal judge and even the expert as to what it needs. As I understand it, it concerns itself with following through when airplanes, guns or tanks, for example, are being built. It follows through and keeps in touch with the work. It is that relationship between it and defence production, which the minister says is in
Canadian Commercial Corporation charge of these things, that I want to get at. What does the minister consider is the division of responsibility?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: Relations between the Department of National Defence and the Department of Defence Production remain unchanged. Requisitions come from the deputy minister of national defence to the deputy minister of defence production. How they are handled in the Department of Defence Production is a matter of departmental organization with which the military side is not concerned. The division of the work of the two departments is that the defence department specifies what is required. They say what they want, when they want it and where they want it. In other words, any plans prepared for buildings are prepared by the Department of National Defence. Any specifications for goods to be purchased for the Department of National Defence are prepared by that department.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: Let us take airplanes.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: They set out the type of airplane. Of course the actual development of airplanes is not carried out directly by the Department of National Defence, but nevertheless that department sets out the over-all specifications and works with the Department of Defence Production in following the development through to the final mock-up. After that it becomes a matter solely for defence production. However, the Department of National Defence has another function, that of inspection. In other words, the Department of National Defence must say that the article is satisfactory. For that purpose there is an inspection branch of the Department of National Defence which is responsible for inspection. They say what they want, when and where they want it, and they decide whether the article delivered is up to their specifications. If not, they have the right to reject it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: Does the Department of Defence Production also have inspectors?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: Then it is duplication.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
It is not duplication. There are certain matters that we inspect by agreement, but the final decision as to whether an article is up to specification rests with the Department of National Defence. In some cases, as in the case of aircraft, there is some division of the inspection work, but there is no duplication. There was duplication in the last war. There was plant inspection and the British inspection. That has been eliminated.

Canadian Commercial Corporation While there is inspection of all stages, in some cases by agreement it is performed by inspectors of the Department of Defence Production, and in other cases it is inspectors of the inspection branch of the Department of National Defence.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: Just so I may understand the procedure, do I gather that in the case of a contract for the manufacture in Canada of a certain type of gun or guns such as are under consideration in this case, the Canadian Commercial Corporation would negotiate the contract with the foreign purchaser and carry out the arrangements in Canada for the production of guns on behalf of that foreign purchaser, and that the details then would be worked out by the department for the actual production?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: Then the Department of Defence Production would make the arrangements which were under discussion whereby, in this case, Sorel Industries would plan the actual production in their own plant and in the arsenal which has been taken over?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: In regard to orders from foreign governments, does the external affairs office have to O.K. those orders before they are put through?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, every order for munitions of war placed by a foreign government must obtain the approval of the Department of External Affairs.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
I listened to what the minister said about there being no danger of duplication, and all I can say is that if there is no duplication he is a wizard, because we have all the makings of it. When we started this discussion I did not fully realize the complexity of the situation. I thought we were dealing primarily if not exclusively with the defence department and Canadian Commercial Corporation. Now we have the other organization in the picture, and for the life of me I cannot understand why we need the two other organizations in addition to the Department of National Defence.
The minister has made clear what happens in the case of contracts of certain kinds, and I am not going over that ground again. What he has not made clear, to me at any rate, is why we need these two organizations. I think the minister will agree as a matter of general principle that when you have three or four people working on one job there is prima facie a great danger of duplication, and frankly I do not understand the reason for what is taking place. We have had Canadian Commercial Corporation built up to us as a very useful organization, and let us assume that is so. Now apparently its functions are being diminished; it is to be considerably less important, and we find a new organization coming in. I confess that the matter disturbs me. This afternoon we are going to be asked to amend the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act to give the minister the very fullest powers under it, but we are still left with what seems to me a multiplication of agencies. I would like the minister to tell us further why we need them all.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: Order. Perhaps the point raised by the hon. member for Greenwood could more properly be discussed on the administration item of the estimates of the Department of Defence Production.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: I have listened to the discussion that has gone on for the last few minutes; 1 have read the various sections, and we are in committee of the whole on this bill studying section 1 at the moment. I wonder if at this time it would be in order to discuss the matter of duplication because of the existence of one or two or three corporations. There is no mention in any of the sections of this bill of Defence Construction Limited, for instance. So I think this point should be cleared up if the discussion is to be proceeded with in an orderly fashion.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
With all respect, Mr. Chairman, I think I can put my hon. friend's mind at rest in a few words. Defence Construction certainly is not mentioned in the bill, but I brought it in, and I think perhaps I could make that relationship clear.
First let us take inspection. The duty of inspection technically rests with the Department of National Defence. I think my hon. friend will appreciate why that should be so, because after all the defence department certainly should be entitled to say whether the article for which they are paying is satisfactory.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
And they
have an expert staff to do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, they have a branch of their department for that purpose. However, that branch is not large, and it is not easy to recruit new members quickly. They found that in connection with the inspection of buildings they just did not have the engineering staff available for the purpose; so by arrangement, to which we both agreed, we augmented the inspection staff by recourse to the staff of Central Mortgage. My hon. friend will understand that. Central Mortgage acts as consultants, really, or inspectors for Defence Construction.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
This is
another agency.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
My hon. friend may laugh, but he is accustomed to dealing with corporations. The reason I like corporations is that we know how they keep their books. Everyone understands a corporation; everyone understands a corporate statement. If the departmental organization is carried too far it becomes very difficult to follow. The government's method of keeping books is not the method of a businessman, as my hon. friend will agree; and if we have a big job to do I prefer to handle it in a corporate structure where bookkeeping methods are well defined and well understood by everyone. That is the reason for the two corporations.
As to the point in which my hon. friend is interested, while the corporation we are
Canadian Commercial Corporation discussing here was a very effective means of handling defence requirements in peacetime, it is not capable of expanding to the extent required to take care of new productive facilities and all the ramifications of a $5 billion defence program to be completed in three years. What we have done is take from this corporation certain functions such as aircraft production, gun production, chemical production and so on, which it formerly performed; and these are now peformed by branches set up for those specific purposes. I hope I have made myself clear.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, the minister has made it dear, but I still want to ask this. He has told us there is a competent engineering staff in the Department of National Defence who lay out the work to be done, who follow it through and inspect it. Am I right in assuming there is also a competent engineering staff in defence production? Will the minister speak on that?
Then, we have had it indicated to us that the Canadian Commercial Corporation has been shorn of a good many of its functions. The question naturally arises, and I am appreciating what the minister said about his preference for corporation books rather than government books, but it does not necessarily follow you need two corporations instead of one just for that purpose. Why could not either the Canadian Commercial Corporation have been given the necessary expert assistance to do what is now being done by defence production or vice versa? Why could not defence production take over the whole thing? Is there a natural division between the two?
I come back to my first question. Will the minister say what engineering staff there is in defence production, and whether or not there is any in the Canadian Commercial Corporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: The engineering staff of defence production is small, but engineering services available to Defence Construction Limited are retained for the purpose of inspecting construction.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: They remain in the Canadian Commercial Corporation or the other company?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: They are retained by Defence Construction Limited. Defence Construction Limited' is responsible for the building carried out by the armed forces, and Defence Construction Limited retains the engineering services that are made available to it by Central Mortgage and Housing.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
That is
merely to do that building?

Canadian Commercial Corporation

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
I think a
while ago we were considering the functions of defence production in connection with aeroplanes and things like that.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
Well, an aeroplane order is
handled by the production branch of the department. There is a branch that devotes itself exclusively to the production of aircraft, and they have everything to do with the production of aircraft.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
That is the
Department of National Defence.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: No, the Department of Defence Production.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
But the
minister has already told us that the Department of National Defence also concerns itself with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
They decide what aircraft
they want, and they follow the production through to determine they are getting it. They perform certain inspection services, the major inspection services in that particular case.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
I understand the difficulty of
the chairman in regard to the field that this is covering, but I would point out that section 1 which is under consideration is the general section, and also the section which defines the minister under this particular act as the Minister of Defence Production. I believe, therefore, that this is the one place where we can get some rationalization of the need for the amendment, and also possibly the question as to whether other amendments might even be desirable from the point of view of simplifying the relationship between these different bodies.
From what has taken place, I understand that the Department of National Defence, as a government department, is making decisions in regard to military requirements, as a result of which certain contracts are then made by other agencies. These agencies may be the Department of Defence Production, acting as a department, or the Canadian Commercial Corporation or Defence Construction Limited, both of which corporations come under the same minister. The thing which I find it difficult to understand is why, with the immensely wide powers conferred upon the Department of Defence Production, it is necessary to have the Canadian Commercial Corporation at all. Secondly, why, if it is necessary to have the Canadian Commercial Corporation, it is necessary also to have Defence Production Limited, in view of the extremely wide powers that are conferred and would be extended by this amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
It is not essential, but it is desirable we think. In the last war we had a similar corporation which was called War Supplies Limited. War Supplies Limited handled all contracts made by the United States government or other governments with the Canadian government. These contracts were processed by the old department of munitions and supply. It is much easier for a foreign government to do business with a corporation having offices in the country than it is to do business between governments. The latter is more cumbersome. War Supplies Limited had an office in Washington, and I think the Washington office handled $2 million or $3 million worth of United States orders that were carried out in Canada. It also had an office in London.
The Canadian Commercial Corporation has offices in Washington, London and several offices across Canada. Instead of winding up this corporation, which we could have done, we have made it responsible for booking foreign orders and for handling foreign business. Those are pretty well its duties today. They have been whittled down to that, but it is still handling very large orders and is performing a useful function. The staff of the department has largely been transferred over into one of the production departments or into the general purchasing departments of defence production.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: I observe it is almost six o'clock, but I am going to suggest that I believe it would help us in considering this complicated and rather perplexing problem if we could have a fist of the staff of each of the organizations we have been talking about this afternoon. When I say a "list", I am not concerned with having every name but I do want to have a convenient list showing how many engineers, accountants and what-not are available, so we shall get an idea of how much talent there is, and how it is divided.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: Perhaps I could answer the question about personnel right now. There seems to be a little misconception about the bill. The staff of the corporation in March of this year was some 660. I do not know what it is today but if it is not down in the neighbourhood of 40 it will be down to that in a matter of a few weeks. Perhaps that will give an effective picture as well as anything.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
I meant
something more than that. I meant the Canadian Commercial Corporation, defence production, defence construction-of course, when you come to national defence, I realize

one must limit it there. I suppose we should have whatever is the relevant unit there, the engineering unit or whatever it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: I am trying to be reasonable, but we are discussing a corporation that has a personnel of about 40. My hon. friend wants to bring in a list of the personnel of the Department of Defence Production that probably has a staff of 1,200. Let us keep the proportion. If the committee wishes to discuss the estimates of the department, we shall be glad to give you the names and talents of each man. I do not know who is an engineer, and who is a lawyer, but I do not think it is pertinent to this particular bill. I am quite willing to show the relationship of this corporation to anything the hon. member likes, but I am not prepared to discuss the Department of Defence Production as a whole on this bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: Could I just make this point. After all, it is true we are now considering an amendment to the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act, but nevertheless it brings in very directly the Department of Defence Production because the Minister of Defence Production is going to exercise some powers under this act. It may be, evidently it is the case, that the Canadian Commercial Corporation has become very much smaller, and in one sense the minister may say we are trying to get all the detail we can. It seems to me it is a perfectly natural thing for us to ask these questions because I do not see how we can properly consider a smaller and shrunken Canadian Commercial Corporation unless we know why it is shrunken and what is the cause of its present situation, and I hope the minister will take that view. It seems to me this is a convenient time to do it. It is a thing that might very naturally happen here. I do not see why it should not happen here as well as elsewhere. The same questions will be asked and answered by the same people.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: I will ask the chairman to think over the ruling. If he can think of any reason why I should explain the Department of Defence Production on this bill I shall be very pleased to do it at the next sitting.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
I have great confidence in the chairman. I hope he will think of a good reason.
Section stands.
